title: Proactive Defense Against Quishing: Integrating Predictive Analytics and Dynamic Analysis for Intelligent Threat Detection
model_family: boosted trees; classical ML; hybrid static-dynamic system
dataset: 3,353 unique QR-derived URLs with benign and phishing samples; decoded, preprocessed, enriched with lexical and WHOIS metadata; subset of 10 high-risk URLs dynamically sandboxed for behavioral analysis
evaluation_metrics: AUC; accuracy; precision; calibration curve; SHAP feature importance; sandbox evidence counts; analyst-interface workflow evidence
baseline_models: Static lexical-only LightGBM; Static+WHOIS LightGBM
explanation_purpose: explain QR-derived URL risk through SHAP feature attributions, calibrated probabilities, WHOIS features, sandbox artifacts, screenshots, and Streamlit analyst interface outputs
main_findings: The LightGBM quishing detector reports strong domain-holdout performance: lexical-only model AUC 0.984, accuracy 96.1%, precision 95.3%; Static+WHOIS model accuracy 96.7%, precision 96.2%, and mean AUC around 0.98, although the table lists AUC 0.949 for Static+WHOIS while surrounding text describes improved stability. SHAP identifies domain_age_days, url_length, is_https, and num_special_chars as important predictors. Operational/forensic utility is partly measured through system integration: Playwright sandboxing captures redirects, HTTP codes, forms, scripts, and screenshots; among 10 sandboxed URLs, nine show phishing features. A Streamlit analyst interface unifies QR upload, decoded URL, lexical/WHOIS features, confidence, SHAP plots, sandbox evidence, and report generation.
limitations: Dynamic sandbox validation is demonstrated on only 10 URLs. No latency, throughput, or live SOC field study is reported. The AUC reporting is internally inconsistent between Table I and explanatory text. Trust/analyst efficiency claims are not backed by measured analyst outcomes.
reproducibility_notes: The pipeline components are specified: QR decoding, lexical and WHOIS feature extraction, LightGBM, Playwright sandbox, SHAP, and Streamlit dashboard. Dataset provenance and code availability are not clearly provided in the extracted text.
threats_to_validity: Small sandbox sample limits behavioral-validation claims. Domain-holdout evaluation may not represent QR campaign diversity. Interface usefulness is argued from design rather than tested with analysts. Metric inconsistency should be tracked in synthesis.
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: operational interface support. Mixed-purpose xAI: no. Trust evidence: none/rhetorical. Operational evidence: prototype/interface. Validation gate: interface. Reproducibility: low. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.
model_families_normalized: classical ML; boosted trees; hybrid ML/DL
trust_evidence_basis: Analyst-interface usefulness is argued from design only.
operational_evidence_basis: Streamlit dashboard and sandbox artifacts are demonstrated on a small dynamic subset.
claim_evidence_mismatch: Prototype evidence is real but small; trust and operational-scale claims remain overextended.
coding_notes: Quishing study with SHAP and dynamic-analysis evidence.

title: XAI-PhD: Fortifying Trust of Phishing URL Detection Empowered by Shapley Additive Explanations
model_family: boosted trees
dataset: ISCX-URL2016 filtered to benign+phishing URLs (45,343 rows from the 114,250-record source corpus; 35,343 benign and 10,000 phishing after filtering)
evaluation_metrics: accuracy; precision; recall; F1-measure; running prediction time per whole dataset; running prediction time per record
baseline_models: DT; SVM; KNN; prior literature comparators
explanation_purpose: feature attribution for post-hoc global/local explanation plus SHAP-guided feature selection to reduce model complexity and justify predictions
main_findings: Uses SHAP to rank 18 lexical URL features, retains 10 influential features, and trains a LightGBM phishing URL detector on the filtered ISCX-URL2016 corpus under 10-fold cross-validation. The paper reports 99.8% accuracy, 100% precision, 99% recall, and 100% F1, while also presenting measured efficiency evidence: prediction time drops from 2.48 ms to 1.47 ms per record when SHAP-based feature reduction is used (reported 40.73% improvement), with whole-dataset runtime also slightly reduced. Explanation outputs include SHAP summary, heatmap, interaction, waterfall, and force-style visual analyses that show how url_len, url_path_len, fld_len, count_dirs, punctuation, and related lexical cues shape predictions at global and instance level.
limitations: Interpretability is tightly intertwined with feature selection rather than a purely separable post-hoc explanation layer; evaluation is limited to one filtered benchmark dataset and offline cross-validation with no external or live deployment validation; trust is framed rhetorically through transparency/credibility language rather than measured through human-subject or analyst studies; lexical URL features may be brittle under adaptive phishing evolution
reproducibility_notes: No code repository or executable artifact release is stated in the extracted full text; dataset provenance, hardware specifications (ThinkPad E560; 16 GB RAM; Windows 10), and cross-validation setup are reported clearly
threats_to_validity: Operational evidence is measured and relatively strong at the model/runtime level, but human-facing trust evidence is absent; results remain benchmark-bound and do not establish analyst effectiveness or field robustness
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: explanation-informed modeling. Mixed-purpose xAI: yes-feature-selection. Trust evidence: none/rhetorical. Operational evidence: runtime/resource. Validation gate: artifact. Reproducibility: moderate. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.
trust_evidence_basis: Trust remains rhetorical.
operational_evidence_basis: Prediction time per dataset and per record is reported.
claim_evidence_mismatch: Runtime evidence is model-level; analyst effectiveness and field robustness are not measured.
coding_notes: SHAP feature-selection study with reported runtime measurements.

title: E2Phish: Explainable Ensemble Machine Learning Model for Enhanced Phishing URL Detection
model_family: ensemble ML; stacking; voting; classical ML
dataset: Public Kaggle phishing URL dataset (10,000 rows, 50 columns including target variable; balanced legitimate/phishing labels; Mutual Information selects top 32 features)
evaluation_metrics: accuracy; precision; recall; F1-score
baseline_models: Decision Tree; Naive Bayes; Logistic Regression; SVM; hard voting; soft voting; stacking ensemble
explanation_purpose: Post-hoc explanation of the best stacking ensemble using SHAP beeswarm plots, LIME local explanations, and PDP feature-effect plots; MI feature selection before modeling
main_findings: E2Phish evaluates base classifiers and ensemble variants on a balanced 10,000-row Kaggle phishing URL dataset after Mutual Information selects 32 features. The stacking ensemble is the best reported model with 97% accuracy, 96% precision, 98% recall, and 97% F1, outperforming hard voting and soft voting (both around 93-94% F1/accuracy range) and base models. The XAI module applies SHAP, LIME, and PDP to the best model, identifying PctExtNullSelfRedirectHyperlinksRT/FrequentDomainNameMismatch in SHAP and features such as FrequentDomainName, NumDash, SubmitInfoToEmail, PctNullSelfRedirectHyperlinks, PctExtResourceUrls, and NumDash as important URL-level phishing cues.
limitations: The work remains a benchmark-centered URL study: it uses a single Kaggle dataset, does not report runtime/latency or deployment testing, and does not evaluate whether SHAP/LIME/PDP explanations improve user or analyst decisions. MI feature selection precedes the post-hoc XAI stage, so the explanation workflow is partly coupled to feature-selection logic. The authors acknowledge the need for more heterogeneous and up-to-date phishing URL datasets and note potential computing-resource constraints for ensemble interpretability.
reproducibility_notes: The paper states that project code is available at https://github.com/tejas-kalal/E2Phish and uses a public Kaggle dataset. Model families, algorithms, selected features, and comparison table are described, but hardware/environment details are limited in the extracted full text.
threats_to_validity: Trust/transparency is rhetorical and model-centric rather than empirically measured; operational utility is not addressed beyond code availability and benchmark performance. Generalization to evolving phishing URLs and external datasets remains untested.
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: model inspection. Mixed-purpose xAI: no. Trust evidence: none/rhetorical. Operational evidence: none. Validation gate: artifact. Reproducibility: high. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.
trust_evidence_basis: No human or analyst validation of SHAP/LIME/PDP usefulness.
operational_evidence_basis: No runtime, latency, deployment, or workflow evidence.
claim_evidence_mismatch: Benchmark performance and explanation plots do not support trust or operational claims.

title: LLMs are one-shot URL classifiers and explainers
model_family: transformer/LLM; supervised transformer baseline
posthoc_xai_method: LLM natural-language explanation; LIME comparison proxy
dataset: ISCX-2016 URL dataset, EBBU-2017 URL dataset, and HISPAR-Phishstats (HP) dataset; supervised splits are 60/20/20 with Table 2 counts; LLM evaluation uses 1,000 sampled test URLs per dataset; appendix also evaluates PhiUSIIL
evaluation_metrics: F1; accuracy; precision; recall; Jaccard similarity between LLM self-explanation indicators and LIME indicators; G-Eval readability, coherence, and informativeness
baseline_models: URLTran; URLNet; CatchPhish; PhishRF; LIME explanations from URLTran used as explanation-alignment proxy
explanation_purpose: classify a URL as benign/phishing and generate natural-language self-explanations; compare explanation indicators with LIME indicators from supervised URLTran models
main_findings: GPT-4 Turbo is the best one-shot LLM, with F1 scores of 0.94 on HP, 0.95 on EBBU, and 0.87 on ISCX (average 0.92), about 0.07 below the same-dataset supervised URLTran F1 of 0.99 and within 0.05-0.12 of URLTran in the authors summary. GPT-4 Turbo explanation indicators align with LIME indicators above Jaccard 0.5 for 72% of HP, 69% of EBBU, and 56% of ISCX examples; G-Eval shows most non-LLaMA2 explanations have high readability, coherence, and informativeness. Trust remains rhetorical/automated-quality only: no human user or analyst outcome study is conducted.
limitations: URL-only classification can miss phishing hosted on otherwise legitimate domains because page content is absent. Multi-modal extension would require visiting pages, screenshots, code capture, and LLM queries, introducing latency and fitting server-side rather than end-user-side deployment. API cost drives the 1,000-sample LLM evaluation limit. A user study is proposed but not performed.
reproducibility_notes: Data availability statement says data will be made available on request; no clear public code release is reported in the extracted text. The paper identifies datasets, supervised baselines, model list (GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini, LLaMA 3, LLaMA 2), five repeated LLM queries per URL, and prediction parsing rules.
threats_to_validity: LIME indicators are treated as a proxy gold standard despite known instability and possible mismatch with true human-recognized phishing indicators. G-Eval is automated rather than a human-subject evaluation. LLM background knowledge of benign domains may inflate performance on benchmark URLs and may not generalize to newly registered or private phishing campaigns.
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: local decision rationale. Mixed-purpose xAI: no. Trust evidence: automated proxy. Operational evidence: none. Validation gate: artifact. Reproducibility: moderate. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.
trust_evidence_basis: Jaccard/G-Eval explanation metrics are automated proxies, not measured trust.
operational_evidence_basis: Latency and deployment constraints are discussed as future/server-side concerns.

title: Optimizing Phishing URL Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Feature Counts and Training Times
model_family: classical ML; boosted trees; neural network
dataset: Hannousse and Yahiouche benchmark website-phishing dataset with 11,430 instances, 5,715 legitimate and 5,715 phishing; original dataset has 89 columns / 87 features, but this study uses URL and status columns to derive 41 hexadecimal n-gram statistical features
evaluation_metrics: accuracy; feature-count reduction; training-time speed-up
baseline_models: Hannousse et al. benchmark; Logistic Regression; Random Forest; AdaBoost; XGBoost; Naive Bayes; Neural Network; Decision Tree; LightGBM; Gradient Boosting; CatBoost; ExtraTrees; original 87-feature setting
explanation_purpose: use SHAP global feature attribution and LIME local examples to identify important hexadecimal n-gram features, then reduce feature sets and training time
main_findings: With 41 extracted n-gram features, best reported accuracies include XGBoost 88.15% on 8-grams and LightGBM 87.84% on 8-grams. title: Addressing feature selection and extreme learning machine tuning by diversity-oriented social network search: an application for phishing websites detection
model_family: classical ML; extreme learning machine; metaheuristic optimization
dataset: Three public phishing website datasets: Kaggle phishing dataset (10,000 records, 48 features, 5,000 phishing and 5,000 legitimate); UCI phishing websites dataset (11,056 instances, 30 features); UCI Website Phishing small dataset (1,353 instances, 9 features plus target, three classes)

main_findings: The paper proposes a two-level Diversity-Oriented Social Network Search framework where level 1 performs wrapper feature selection and level 2 tunes an Extreme Learning Machine. It evaluates three public phishing website datasets and reports that ELM-DOSNS with feature selection reaches 95.65% accuracy on the Kaggle dataset, 93.94% on the larger UCI phishing websites dataset, and 90.78% on the UCI small dataset; without feature selection, the same approach reaches 97.25%, 94.75%, and 90.04%, respectively. SHAP is applied after model selection to the best ELM-DOSNS model for Kaggle and UCI-small analyses, identifying features such as PctExtHyperlinks, NumNumericChars, NumQueryComponents, PctNullSelfRedirectHyperlinks, FrequentDomainNameMismatch, InsecureForms, SFH, URL_of_Anchor, Request_URL, popUpWindow, URL_Length, and SSL final state as influential phishing indicators.

title: A Multimodal Phishing Website Detection System Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence Technologies
model_family: boosted trees; CNN; transformer/LLM; hybrid ML/DL; LLM
posthoc_xai_method: SHAP; Grad-CAM; LLM natural-language explanation; attention analysis
dataset: Proprietary continuously updated phishing web-resource dataset D1 (about 3.2 million balanced URLs after cleaning: 1.6M phishing and 1.6M legitimate) plus public MTLP dataset D2
evaluation_metrics: F1-score; ROC-AUC; false positive rate; false negative rate; throughput; latency; expert utility ratings; Fleiss kappa; Cronbach alpha
baseline_models: Single-modal CatBoost, CodeBERT, CNN1D, and EfficientNet-B7 branches; multimodal voting variants; external comparison tools Google Safe Browsing, OpenPhish API, and URLhaus API; prior multimodal systems
explanation_purpose: SOC-facing multimodal explanation: SHAP for URL/metadata features, Grad-CAM/integrated gradients for symbolic and visual branches, attention matrices for HTML/CodeBERT, and local LLM/RAG reports that verbalize deterministic XAI outputs
main_findings: This is one of the strongest operational and human-facing papers in the corpus. It implements a late-fusion multimodal phishing web-resource system with CatBoost for URL/metadata, CNN1D for character-level URLs, CodeBERT for HTML, EfficientNet-B7 for screenshots, and a trainable voting/meta-classifier. Reported multimodal F1 is 0.989 on the proprietary updated D1 dataset and 0.953 on the public MTLP dataset. The prototype is implemented as Docker/microservice components integrated with SOC/TI/SIEM tooling, Elasticsearch/Praeco alerting, and Telegram-style notification. Operational evidence includes feature extraction under 8 ms per URL, SHAP computation under 12 ms per URL, CatBoost inference under 8 ms per URL, CodeBERT ONNX around 200 ms, average end-to-end request processing of 47 ms under a 500-URLs/minute test flow, peak load of 1100 URLs/minute without timeouts, and a reported 26% CPU performance gain after compiling CatBoost. The paper also reports zero-day-style testing where 92 of 100 previously unrecorded URLs were flagged suspicious. For trust/utility, 30 explanations were rated by three first-line SOC analysts: mean utility increased from 3.97 to 4.20 with RAG augmentation, Fleiss kappa from 0.82 to 0.84, and Cronbach alpha from 0.90 to 0.96.
limitations: The proprietary D1 dataset and simulated SOC testbed limit external reproducibility; the zero-day experiment is manually/synthetically constructed rather than a longitudinal field deployment. The paper reports some throughput inconsistently across events-per-second and URLs-per-minute language, so operational claims should be cited with care. Late fusion provides modality-specific explanations but does not explain joint cross-modal patterns, and transformer/LLM branches create latency/resource tradeoffs. The analyst evaluation is valuable but small (three analysts, 30 explanations) and measures perceived explanation utility rather than downstream decision accuracy or calibrated trust over time.
reproducibility_notes: Implementation details are unusually rich: Python 3.10, Docker containers, Flask/FastAPI endpoints, MongoDB, Elasticsearch/Praeco, SIEM integration, server specifications (4 Tesla V100 GPUs, 256 GB RAM), model branches, timings, and datasets are described. Public code release is not stated in the extracted full text, and the main D1 dataset appears proprietary/continuously updated.
threats_to_validity: Measured operational evidence and analyst-perceived explanation utility are reported. External replication, full field deployment, and decision-quality outcomes remain limited.
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: operational interface support. Mixed-purpose xAI: no. Trust evidence: explicit human/user/analyst evaluation. Operational evidence: workflow/lifecycle. Validation gate: human interpretation. Reproducibility: moderate. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.
xai_methods_normalized: SHAP; attention/transformer visualization; LLM natural-language explanation; Grad-CAM
model_families_normalized: boosted trees; deep learning; hybrid ML/DL; transformer/LLM; CNN
trust_evidence_basis: Analyst-perceived explanation utility ratings are reported in a simulated SOC/testbed setting.
operational_evidence_basis: Reports throughput/latency/SOC integration evidence, though not a longitudinal field deployment.
claim_evidence_mismatch: Strong operational and analyst evidence is reported, but proprietary data, a synthetic zero-day setting, and inconsistent throughput descriptions constrain broader claims.

title: Knowledge Expansion and Counterfactual Interaction for Reference-Based Phishing Detection
model_family: deep learning; hybrid visual/reference-based system
dataset: DynaPD closed-world dynamic dataset with 6,344 interactable phishing kits and 6,309 Alexa benign webpages; closed-world static Phishpedia benchmark with 29,496 phishing and 30,649 benign URLs/screenshots; CertStream wild-study dataset with 99,000 fresh webpages over 33 days
evaluation_metrics: precision; recall; runtime overhead; knowledge-expansion precision/recall; adversarial robustness mAP/mAR; wild-study precision/recall and real phishing count
baseline_models: PhishIntention; Phishpedia; PhishIntention+BKE; Phishpedia+BKE; WI-only; VirusTotal in wild study
explanation_purpose: expand missing brand references and provide explainable alarms for brandless pages through counterfactual webpage interaction and domain-brand inconsistency evidence
main_findings: DynaPhish improves reference-based phishing detection under live webpage conditions: on DynaPD, PhishIntention recall rises from 40.98% to 68.63% with precision 99.84%, and Phishpedia recall rises from 44.80% to 74.04% with precision 98.97%. Brand Knowledge Expansion alone adds 3,903 references, while Web Interaction alone reaches 43.00% recall at 100.00% precision. In the CertStream wild study, DynaPhish adds 5,294 references and raises PhishIntention recall from 0.10 to 0.71 at precision 1.00, finding 1,327 real phishing webpages versus 127 for PhishIntention alone. Operational utility is measured: median overhead starts around 5.8 sec/page for PhishIntention+DynaPhish and 5.3 sec/page for Phishpedia+DynaPhish, then falls to about 0.5 sec/page as references accumulate; authors recommend separate knowledge-construction and detection threads. Trust is not measured as user trust; five interns label wild-study samples for ground truth rather than evaluating explanation usefulness.
limitations: Effectiveness depends on search-engine retrieval, logo/representation extraction, and logo matching. Non-text logos are harder for representation validation (46% recall versus 83% for text logos), obsolete logos and brandless pages with fake-information-verification cause false negatives, and client/server-side cloaking or CAPTCHA can block interaction. Web Interaction is conservative and incomplete, especially under wild distribution shift.
reproducibility_notes: Code is reported available at https://github.com/code-philia/Dynaphish; DynaPD trial dataset and examples are referenced through the DynaPhish website. Experiments used Ubuntu 20.04.3 LTS with an NVIDIA RTX A4000 GPU; key hyperparameters include representation threshold 0.87, Google retrieval limit k=10, life threshold 3 months, and interaction trial threshold k=3 for experiments / k=1 in the wild study.

Reported predictive performance is extremely high on both Kaggle corpora. LIME provides local explanations for live predictions, while system logs capture requests and explanations. title: Intelligent Cyber Defense: Utilizing Deep Learning for Robust Detection and Prevention of Phishing Websites
model_family: ensemble ML; boosted trees
dataset: Two phishing website datasets: Web Page Phishing Detection Dataset with 11,430 URLs and 87 features (balanced 50/50 phishing-legitimate), and a Phishing Dataset for Machine Learning with about 10,000 webpages, 48 features, collected across Jan/Jun 2015 and May-Jun 2017 using Selenium WebDriver.
evaluation_metrics: Dataset 1: XGBoost accuracy 0.973316, recall 0.971656, precision 0.974245, F1 0.972949, training time 0.780205 s; stacking ensemble accuracy 0.975503. Dataset 2: XGBoost accuracy 0.9895, recall 0.993083, precision 0.986261, F1 0.989660, training time 0.944428 s; stacking ensemble also 0.9895 accuracy.

main_findings: The study benchmarks several tree/ensemble models and finds XGBoost or stacking ensembles strongest across two phishing website datasets. title: LightPhishAI: A Lightweight Multimodal Feature Extraction and Fusion Framework for Real-Time Phishing Detection on IoT Devices
model_family: deep learning; CNN; transformer/LLM; hybrid ML/DL
posthoc_xai_method: Grad-CAM; SHAP; LIME; attention-based modality attribution
dataset: multimodal phishing/benign data from PhishTank and OpenPhish for phishing, Tranco top sites for benign URLs, UCI PhiUSIIL for URL/metadata validation, and Phish-IRIS screenshot corpus for vision validation; each sample aligns URL, screenshot, and metadata; stratified 70/15/15 split
evaluation_metrics: accuracy; precision/recall implied; F1; AUC; GPU latency; edge latency; parameter count; model size; FLOPs; CPU utilization; power; energy per inference; ablation/fusion comparison
baseline_models: text-only TinyBERT/GRU; image-only MobileNetV2/CNN; metadata-only MLP; early fusion; late fusion; BERT-base+MobileNetV2; TinyBERT+MobileNetV2

main_findings: PhishFusionNet adaptive-attention fusion achieves the best tabled performance among baselines with 95.0% accuracy, 94.2% F1, and 97.9% AUC, outperforming text-only TinyBERT/GRU (90.3% accuracy, 89.1% F1) and static fusion schemes; the abstract also reports 98.4% accuracy and 97.9% F1, so synthesis should flag metric inconsistency. Resource measurements include 160-180% mean Raspberry Pi CPU utilization, 4.9W power, and about 0.09J per inference. Explanations localize login/credential regions with Grad-CAM and align SHAP/LIME signals around domain age, SSL, WHOIS, IP address, URL length, and suspicious tokens.

reproducibility_notes: Experimental setup is detailed: Intel i9-12900K, 64GB RAM, RTX 4090, Python 3.10, PyTorch 2.2, CUDA 12.1, ONNX Runtime 1.17, Raspberry Pi 4, 70/15/15 split, batch size 32, 30 epochs, Adam, cosine decay, warm-up, early stopping. No public code repository is evident in the extracted text.
threats_to_validity: Cross-source multimodal alignment and screenshot acquisition may introduce selection artifacts. Edge measurements may depend heavily on implementation and ONNX optimizations. Metric inconsistency requires cautious synthesis. Trust claims are not human-validated.
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: model inspection. Mixed-purpose xAI: no. Trust evidence: none/rhetorical. Operational evidence: runtime/resource. Validation gate: artifact. Reproducibility: moderate. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.

title: Explainable and Adversarially Evaluated CNN for Visual Phishing Detection
model_family: CNN; MobileNetV2; visual deep learning
dataset: Balanced high-resolution screenshot dataset combining phishing screenshots from the Mendeley Phishing Detection Dataset with manually captured legitimate screenshots from government, banking, and e-commerce websites; images resized to 224 x 224 and normalized.
evaluation_metrics: Accuracy, adversarial robustness, confidence drop, parameters, and inference latency. MobileNetV2 reports 95.2% accuracy and 2.4M parameters; baselines: Logistic Regression 84.2%, Random Forest 86.1%, Shallow CNN 91.3%. Adversarial tests on 20 samples: no attack 0/20 misclassified, FGSM epsilon=0.01 misclassifies 3/20 with 22.5% confidence drop, PGD 40 steps misclassifies 6/20 with 35.8% confidence drop. Inference time is about 48 ms per screenshot on a single system.
baseline_models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Shallow CNN, and MobileNetV2; optional pipeline mentions Vision Transformer and ResNet as selectable models but table centers on MobileNetV2.
explanation_purpose: LIME visual overlays identify screenshot regions such as logos, login fields, irregular buttons, misaligned forms, or low-quality logos that influence phishing/legitimate predictions.
main_findings: the paper is a valuable visual-phishing entry because it combines MobileNetV2 screenshot classification, LIME visual explanation, and adversarial testing with FGSM/PGD. MobileNetV2 outperforms classical and shallow CNN baselines while remaining relatively lightweight. The robustness experiment shows that imperceptible perturbations materially reduce confidence and cause misclassification, especially under PGD. Operational utility is measured as single-system inference latency (~48 ms/screenshot) and model size, but real-world browser/API/hardware latency is explicitly not validated. Trust is discussed as improved transparency for users/auditors but no human-subject or analyst study is reported.
limitations: Dataset size/generalizability remain limited; future work targets VisPhish/PhishINTEL expansion, stronger adaptive attacks such as DeepFool/Carlini-Wagner/AutoAttack, practitioner benchmarking, browser add-on/lightweight app deployment, real-world latency testing, multimodal signals, and human-centric interpretability studies.
reproducibility_notes: Reports dataset sources, preprocessing image size, model architecture, baselines, accuracy table, adversarial test settings/results, model parameter count, and single-system inference latency. Code availability was not identified in the extracted full text.
threats_to_validity: Single-system latency may not transfer to browser/API deployment; adversarial evaluation uses a small 20-sample attack summary and excludes stronger adaptive attacks; LIME overlays are not validated against user/analyst outcomes.

operational_evidence_basis: Inference latency and parameter count are reported.

title: AQUAPHISH: Leveraging Metaheuristics and Automated Machine Learning for Precision Phishing Detection
model_family: ensemble ML; AutoML; boosted trees
dataset: Mendeley Data phishing website dataset (10,000 records; 5,000 phishing and 5,000 legitimate; 48 URL/domain/technical features reduced to 36 with WOA; 80/20 split)
evaluation_metrics: accuracy; precision; recall; F1-score; ROC-AUC; MSE; RMSE; MAE; R2; runtime; inference latency
baseline_models: PSO + Random Forest; GA + SVM; DNN + manual feature selection; H2O AutoML candidate GBM/XGBoost/deep learning/stacked ensemble models; prior literature comparators
explanation_purpose: SHAP-based post-hoc feature attribution for phishing risk scores and transparency analysis of URL/domain indicators; WOA performs feature reduction independently of SHAP.
main_findings: AQUAPHISH reframes phishing website detection as a regression-style risk-scoring task, reduces 48 URL/domain/technical features to 36 with Whale Optimization Algorithm, and uses H2O AutoML to select stacked ensemble models. Reported classification-style performance is strong after thresholding the risk score (accuracy 98.60%, precision 98.36%, recall 97.25%, F1 97.77%, AUC 0.991), with regression metrics also reported across AutoML runtime budgets (best cited R2 0.9534 with RMSE 0.1079). The paper gives unusually concrete operational evidence: average training time falls from 117 s to 84 s after feature reduction, leaderboard runtime improves by 23.6%, inference time per sample is reduced by about 18%, and the conclusion reports about 22 ms per instance plus possible H2O MOJO/cloud/edge deployment. SHAP is used on the top-performing XGBoost/ensemble pipeline to identify SSLfinal_State, URL_of_Anchor, Request_URL, Having_Sub_Domain, and Web_Traffic as influential phishing-risk factors.
limitations: Mixed-purpose xAI: SHAP is a post-hoc explanation layer for the final model, but the overall contribution is tightly coupled to feature reduction and AutoML optimization. Evaluation uses one public dataset and static URL/webpage features; adversarial manipulation, dynamic content, online drift, and real browser/SOC deployment are not empirically tested. Trustworthiness is asserted through transparency language and analyst/end-user usefulness claims, but no human-subject or analyst outcome study is reported.
reproducibility_notes: Dataset availability is explicit via the Mendeley repository listed in the paper; the dataset composition, 80/20 split, WOA feature count, H2O AutoML setup, runtime budgets, and deployment mechanism via H2O MOJO are described. No standalone source-code repository is stated in the extracted full text.
threats_to_validity: Operational evidence is measured at the model/runtime level but remains laboratory profiling rather than live deployment evidence. No user, analyst, or human-subject evaluation is reported, so human trust is not treated as measured.
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: model inspection. Mixed-purpose xAI: no. Trust evidence: none/rhetorical. Operational evidence: runtime/resource. Validation gate: artifact. Reproducibility: moderate. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.

operational_evidence_basis: Runtime and inference-latency profiling plus H2O MOJO deployment path.
claim_evidence_mismatch: Operational profiling is real, but trust/deployment claims exceed human or live evidence.

title: WebSecAsst - A Machine Learning based Chrome Extension
model_family: boosted trees; XGBoost; browser-extension workflow
dataset: UCI Phishing Websites dataset with 30 attributes and 2,456 instances; 24 attributes used after excluding features infeasible for local collection such as port, on_mouseover, popUpWindow, PageRank, links-pointing-to-page, and statistical report.
evaluation_metrics: Accuracy and confusion-matrix counts. XGBoost accuracy 96.698%; Random Forest 95.838%; KNN n=3 94.029%, n=5 93.668%, n=7 92.220%. Confusion counts: XGBoost TN 934, FP 39, FN 34, TP 1204; RF TN 938, FP 61, FN 31, TP 1181.
baseline_models: XGBoost final model compared with Random Forest and KNN variants; VirusTotal API is used for downloaded-file hash checks.
explanation_purpose: SHAP global feature importance explains the XGBoost website classifier. Top features include URL_of_Anchor, SSLfinal_State, Shortining_Service, web_traffic, and Prefix_Suffix.
main_findings: WebSecAsst is one of the few included papers with an implemented operational workflow. It builds a Chrome extension that sends the current URL to a local endpoint, extracts HTML/JavaScript/certificate features locally, classifies the site with XGBoost, and separately hashes downloaded files for VirusTotal checking. XGBoost achieves 96.698% accuracy on the UCI phishing dataset and is interpreted with SHAP global feature importance. The design makes a concrete privacy/deployment claim because website analysis runs locally and only file hashes leave the machine. Trust is not measured with users; privacy and user-assistance claims are rhetorical/architectural. Operational utility is measured as implemented extension workflow and demonstrated examples, though latency/resource benchmarks are absent.
limitations: The extension currently works only on Debian-based systems. The website classifier uses a small older UCI feature dataset and excludes several features because they are infeasible or inaccessible locally. No latency, scalability, or user usability study is reported.
reproducibility_notes: Provides dataset source, feature-selection rationale, accuracy/confusion tables, SHAP feature list, local Apache/PHP/Python architecture, endpoint behavior, VirusTotal file-hash workflow, and GitHub links for setup and scripts.
threats_to_validity: Small/older UCI dataset may not represent modern phishing; local feature extraction differs from the original dataset feature space; no human trust/usability evidence; operational deployment is demonstrated but not benchmarked for latency or robustness.
synthesis_notes: Explanation role: operational interface support. Mixed-purpose xAI: no. Trust evidence: none/rhetorical. Operational evidence: prototype/interface. Validation gate: interface. Reproducibility: high. Claim-evidence risk: moderate.

title: Phishing Website Detection Model Construction Based on Improved IHHO-RF-SHAP Algorithm
model_family: Random Forest; optimization-assisted ensemble ML; IHHO-RF
dataset: UCI standard phishing website dataset filtered for outliers/missing values to 1,353 records: 548 legitimate, 702 phishing, and 103 suspicious. Nine website indicators are used: IP address, pop-up window, Request URL, misuse/fake HTTPS, URL of anchor, website traffic, server form handler, age of domain, and long URL. Train/test split is 75/25.
evaluation_metrics: Benchmark-function optimization statistics for IHHO vs HHO and qualitative phishing-classification comparison. IHHO uses population size 20 and 50 iterations for RF hyperparameter optimization of ntree, mtry, and mdepth; the paper states IHHO-RF has faster convergence and improved classification performance over HHO-RF, but numeric phishing-detection accuracy/precision/recall/F1 values are not extractable from the text beyond figure-level claims.

explanation_purpose: Global SHAP analysis aggregates values across data points to identify key drivers of phishing detection, with SFH (Server Form Handler) as the most important indicator followed by fake HTTPS, pop-ups, URL of anchor, long URL, Request URL, age of domain, website traffic, and IP-address legitimacy.
main_findings: the study couples improved Harris Hawks Optimization with Random Forest for phishing website detection, then applies SHAP as a post-hoc global explanation layer. The main evidence is that IHHO improves optimization stability and convergence on benchmark functions and is claimed to improve/faster-converge against HHO-RF for phishing detection. SHAP identifies SFH as the dominant phishing indicator and provides an interpretable feature ranking over nine website indicators. Trust/user adoption is claimed rhetorically without user evaluation. Operational utility is inferred from faster convergence and practical-value claims, but runtime, latency, deployment, and numeric classification metrics are not reported in extractable form.
limitations: The paper does not provide extractable numeric phishing-detection performance in the text, relies on a filtered UCI benchmark with only nine indicators, and emphasizes optimization/convergence more than external validation or deployment evidence.

title: Explainable TabNet ensemble model for identification of obfuscated URLs with features selection to ensure secure web browsing
model_family: hybrid deep learning + ensemble ML; TabNet stacking ensemble
dataset: Public URL-2016/CIC-style multi-class URL dataset with 79 features and five classes (benign, spam, phishing, malware, defacement), including more than 35,300 benign, 12,000 spam, about 10,000 phishing, more than 11,500 malware, and about 45,450 defacement URLs.
evaluation_metrics: TabNet ensemble accuracy 97.8%, precision 0.978, recall 0.976, F1 0.978, Kappa about 0.968/0.96. 10-fold cross-validation mean accuracy 97.27% with 95% CI width 0.004. Imbalance experiments preserve phishing precision/recall around 0.94/0.96.

title: Mitigating Cyber Threats: Machine Learning and Explainable AI for Phishing Detection
model_family: classical ML; CNN; boosted trees
dataset: Four public URL datasets: ISCX-URLs (9,965 phishing, 35,378 non-phishing), PL-URLs (700 phishing, 300 non-phishing), PhishGuard URLs (25,100 phishing, 35,017 non-phishing), and Suspicious-URLs (25,000 phishing, 25,070 non-phishing). Eleven engineered hyperlink/URL features are extracted.

title: Enhanced Phishing Payload Detection Using Fine-Tuned DistilBERT and XAI-Based NLP Models
model_family: transformer/DistilBERT; classical ML baselines
dataset: Zefang-liu public phishing-email-dataset with 18,650 labeled emails and columns for Email Text and Email Type. Preprocessing includes lowercasing, punctuation/special-character and stopword removal, WordPiece tokenization, stratified splitting, SMOTE for imbalance, and TextAttack-generated adversarial examples.
evaluation_metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC-ROC, 3-fold validation, confusion matrix, and adversarial success rate. DistilBERT reports 98.52% accuracy and AUC 0.9993; confusion matrix: 4,434 safe and 2,909 phishing correctly classified, 95 safe false positives, 15 phishing false negatives. 3-fold accuracy: 98.60%, 98.58%, 98.52%; 3-fold AUC: 0.9992, 0.9991, 0.9990. Traditional baseline AUCs: RF 0.996, LR 0.995, KNN 0.993, SVM 0.991, Gradient Boosting 0.989, AdaBoost 0.972, NB 0.939, Decision Tree 0.912. Adversarial success rate is 11.2% for phishing samples and 4.7% for safe emails.
baseline_models: Random Forest, Logistic Regression, KNN, SVM, Gradient Boosting, AdaBoost, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, and DistilBERT.
explanation_purpose: Token-level LIME and SHAP explanations identify text spans/terms driving phishing or safe-email predictions; used to inspect misclassification and adversarial obfuscation patterns.
main_findings: the paper fine-tunes DistilBERT for phishing payload/email-text detection, adds adversarial training, and uses LIME/SHAP for token-level interpretation. DistilBERT substantially leads the accuracy chart and achieves AUC 0.9993, with stable three-fold metrics and a low false-negative count. Error analysis links mistakes to obfuscated links, benign financial phrasing, Unicode manipulation, and marketing-like urgency terms. Adversarial evaluation finds higher vulnerability for phishing samples than safe emails. Trust is framed as transparency/usability for security analysis, but no human or analyst evaluation is reported. Operational utility is not measured; live email-client plugins, online deployment trials, and runtime reduction are future work.
limitations: Findings are limited to one public email dataset and email-based phishing payloads. dataset: PhishTank phishing URLs, about 38,000 instances with 8 original fields, plus University of New Brunswick legitimate URLs, about 35,000 authentic URLs; final model uses 21 extracted URL features.
evaluation_metrics: accuracy; precision; recall; F1-score; training/testing loss and accuracy; SHAP global hierarchy, decision plot, and waterfall plot.
baseline_models: Multiple conventional ML models plus prior CNN/GCNN literature comparators.
explanation_purpose: explain which engineered URL features drive the CNN's phishing predictions.
main_findings: The proposed 1D CNN reports 99.85% accuracy and 99.80% F1-score, outperforming benchmark ML models and prior works in the paper's comparison. SHAP DeepExplainer identifies URL Length and Hostname length as high-impact features, with other URL-count and indexing indicators contributing less.
limitations: No explicit limitations section is extracted; evaluation relies on URL-only features and public source data; user interaction and emerging threat behavior are not assessed.
reproducibility_notes: Dataset sources, 21 feature-extraction criteria, CNN layer table, and SHAP DeepExplainer sample size of 5,000 are described.
threats_to_validity: Very high benchmark accuracy may reflect source separability; daily changing PhishTank data and URL-only features may limit future reproducibility and generalization.
